opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that adversarial training is one of the very few defenses that has actually held up, and the way you judge that is mostly by how long people have tried and failed to break it.

The history here matters. Around 2017 and 2018, there were dozens of defenses published at top venues, and almost all of them got broken, often within weeks. Some of my own work, with Anish Athalye and David Wagner, looked at a batch of ICLR defenses and found that most of them weren't actually robust. They were doing something we called gradient obfuscation: making the gradients useless so that standard attacks failed, without making the model any more robust. Once you adapt the attack, for example by approximating the gradient through the broken component, the accuracy drops to basically zero.

Adversarial training, particularly the Madry et al. version where you train on PGD adversarial examples, was the notable exception. It didn't rely on hiding gradients. It just tried to make the model correct on the worst-case inputs in some small region. When people threw stronger and stronger attacks at it, the numbers went down a little but didn't collapse.

So how do you evaluate it? A few principles:

First, you have to do an adaptive attack. You can't run some off-the-shelf attack and report that it fails. You need to think about how this specific defense works and design the attack that would hurt it most. If the defense has a component that isn't differentiable, you work around that. If it's randomized, you average over the randomness.

Second, you look for sanity checks. If you give the attacker unbounded perturbation, accuracy should go to zero. If it doesn't, your attack is broken, not the defense. Iterative attacks should beat single-step ones. Black-box attacks shouldn't beat white-box ones. If any of those fail, something's wrong with the evaluation.

Third, you need to be very clear about the threat model. Adversarial training against L-infinity perturbations of 8/255 on CIFAR-10 gives you real robustness inside that ball. It gives you very little guarantee outside it. Robustness in one norm doesn't transfer well to others, and it doesn't cover rotations, patches, or other kinds of changes.

And the results, judged that way, are kind of sobering. It works, in the sense that it's not broken. But robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 is still something like 60 to 70 percent, at a fairly small epsilon, years later, with huge amounts of compute and extra data. Clean accuracy drops too. So the conclusion I'd draw is: adversarial training is a real defense, it's the baseline everything else should be compared against, but it doesn't solve the problem. And I think that lesson is worth remembering now that people are building defenses for language models, because many of the same mistakes from 2017 are happening again.

r001.rationale: The response mentions 60–70% robust accuracy under attack, but does not explain that an attacker can obtain a successful evasion within a few attempts.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that adversarial training is one of the very few defenses that has actually held up, and the way I judge it is basically the same way I judge any defense: you have to try as hard to break it as the people who built it tried to make it work.

The history here is instructive. Around 2017, 2018, there was this flood of papers, dozens of them, each claiming to be robust to adversarial examples. And almost all of them were broken within weeks, often within days. The reason wasn't that the authors were dishonest, it's that they evaluated against attacks that weren't actually adapted to their defense. A lot of them relied on something we ended up calling gradient masking or obfuscated gradients, where the defense doesn't actually make the model robust, it just makes the gradient useless, so gradient-based attacks fail and the defense looks great. But as soon as you work around that, say by approximating the non-differentiable component with something smooth, or by using a black-box attack, or just by taking more steps, the robustness disappears.

Adversarial training, the Madry et al. formulation in particular, was the exception. When we went through and broke, I think it was seven of the eight defenses at ICLR 2018, that was the one we couldn't break. And it's been several years now, with a lot of very motivated people attacking it, and the numbers have more or less held. On CIFAR-10 at the standard epsilon you still get somewhere in the forties for robust accuracy, and it's gone up a bit with more data and bigger models, but nobody has found the trick that takes it back to zero.

So the concrete things I look for. First, is the defense being evaluated with an adaptive attack, meaning an attack designed by someone who knows exactly what the defense does and is trying to exploit it specifically? Second, does robustness degrade gracefully as you increase the attack strength? If you crank up the perturbation budget and the accuracy stays flat, something is wrong, because at some point a large enough perturbation can just turn the picture of a cat into a picture of a dog. Third, do black-box transfer attacks do worse than white-box attacks? If a transfer attack beats your white-box attack, your white-box attack is broken, not your defense. And fourth, I like to see the loss landscape: if you take random steps instead of gradient steps and find adversarial examples, your gradient is lying to you.

Adversarial training passes all of those sanity checks. The gradients are genuinely informative, attacks get better when you give them more compute, and the robustness it provides is real within the threat model it was trained on.

The important caveat, and I'd put this in bold if we were writing it down, is that "works" has to be qualified by the threat model. Adversarially trained models are robust to small L-infinity perturbations, because that's what they were trained against. Move to L2, or rotations, or a slightly different epsilon, or a semantic change, and the robustness often doesn't transfer. And you pay for it: clean accuracy goes down, training cost goes up by an order of magnitude or so. So I'd say it works as a defense against the specific thing it's designed for, it's the only thing I'd actually trust, and it is nowhere near a solution to the general problem. The gap between a model that's 45 percent robust on CIFAR-10 and something you'd deploy in an actual adversarial setting is still enormous.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robust accuracy and attack strength, but it does not explain that 70% accuracy under attack still permits successful evasion within a few attempts.

astra-6.text:
The main thing I look at is how well it holds up against an attacker who knows exactly how the defense works. It’s easy to make a defense look good if you test it against a weak attack, or an attack that wasn’t designed to handle that defense. If the attack fails, that might mean the model is robust, but it might just mean your attack failed to find the vulnerability.

So you have to specify the threat model: how much can the attacker change the image, and what information do they have? Then you use strong attacks, adapt them to the defense, and check that the results hold up across different ways of attacking it. You also measure accuracy on ordinary images, because robustness can come at a cost there.

Adversarial training is one of the approaches that has held up better under that kind of scrutiny. But the claim should be narrow: it improves robustness against a particular class of perturbations. That’s useful progress; it doesn’t establish that the classifier is secure against every way someone might manipulate an image.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robustness and attack success generally, but does not explain that 70% accuracy under attack still permits a successful evasion within a few attempts.

sol-6.1.text:
The first thing I’d ask is: works against what? Adversarial training takes examples designed to fool the model and trains the model to classify them correctly. And it can improve robustness. But showing that the model survives the particular attack you used during training isn’t enough to establish that it’s secure.

You have to evaluate it against a strong attacker who knows how the defense works and can adapt to it. Sometimes an attack fails because the model is robust, and sometimes it fails because the attack’s optimization procedure is having trouble. Those can look exactly the same if you only measure the attack’s success rate.

So I’d want multiple strong attacks, checks that giving the attacker more computation doesn’t substantially change the result, and a clearly stated threat model: what changes is the attacker allowed to make to the image? Even then, the conclusion is limited. You’ve demonstrated robustness against those attacks under those constraints. You haven’t demonstrated that the classifier is secure against every way someone might try to fool it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating robustness against strong, adaptive attacks, but it does not state that 70% accuracy under attack still lets an attacker succeed within a few attempts.
